Which one do you prefer between The Driver (1978) by Walter Hill Vs Drive (2011) by Nicolas Refn, and why?
The Driver by Walter Hill Vs Drive by Nicolas Refn

Hill's Driver isn't a great picture by any measure, but it exceeds Refn's flick in many ways. Its chase scenes can't quite compare to those that Carey Loftin, Bill Hickman, et al. coordinated and executed in flicks like Bullitt, Vanishing Point, The French Connection, Hickey & Boggs, The Seven-Ups, Thunderbolt and Lightfoot, Smokey and the Bandit, and scores more, but they're nathless superbly shot, cut and performed, cleverly staged, never a moment tedious for their protraction. Refn's chases are slick enough and he sustains tension well, but they're nothing new, and the contemporary hideosity of the cars utilized only seems to emphasize just how perfunctory they feel.

The casting of the prevenient picture is also far superior. Neither O'Neal nor Gosling are who anyone would deem great thespians, but they've both formidable screen presence that's exploited well by their respective directors. However, O'Neal exudes a disciplined menace with a hint of sex appeal wherever Gosling seems merely vacuous. Gosling's dreadfully dull delivery also stultifies him, emphasizing all of his shortcomings as a performer. Mulligan is cute as Gosling's potential love interest, but she's no Adjani, who's as staggeringly gorgeous as personable, not so terribly incongruous in an American genre pic as one would expect and a good match for O'Neal, with whom she shares a modicum of chemistry. Albert Brooks was horribly cast as Refn's kosher villain; he's performed serious roles well before (see Taxi Driver), but he's about as intimidating as a pettish uncle miffed that his favorite parking space was prepossessed at his nephew's mitzvah. Bruce Dern fares much better as Hill's antagonistic detective.

If The Driver's at all underrated despite its little cult, Drive is a strong contender for the single most overestimated movie of the past fifteen years, extolled by audiences of a generation as inscient of cinema as of literature. Refn doesn't belabor his existentialist burden excessively, but his themes and conceits were virtuosically exhausted by Peckinpah, Melville, Frankenheimer, Cimino, Hill, Mann and especially Friedkin decades ago. Drive has some exciting moments and it's generally well-produced, but as an actioner, drama or pastiche, has nothing to offer anyone familiar with this genre from '66 through '95.

Gehinnom is not Hell, but originally a grave and in later times a sort of Purgatory where one is judged based on one's life's deeds, or rather, where one becomes fully aware of one's own shortcomings and negative actions during one's life. The Kabbalah explains it as a "waiting room" (commonly translated as an "entry way") for all souls (not just the wicked). The overwhelming majority of rabbinic thought maintains that people are not in Gehinnom forever; the longest that one can be there is said to be 12 months, however there has been the occasional noted exception.
